newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mourning Algerians bury slain union leader.
newsitem.headline: Mourning Algerians bury slain union leader.

text.p: Thousands of Algerians, including President Liamine Zeroual and army chief Mohamed Lamari, attended the funeral on Thursday of assassinated union leader Abdelhak Benhamouda in Algeria's El-Alia martyrs' cemetery.
Witnesses said the area on the eastern outskirts of Algiers was blanketed in security, with heavily-armed elite troops and plainclothes men on alert.
"He was buried in the same square of graves as president (Mohamed) Boudiaf and (former interior minister) Boubaker Belkaid," one witness said by telephone.

"Zeroual, Mohamed Lamari and Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia and other officials took part," he said. "They all watched silently as the coffin was lowered into the grave after they repeated verses from the (Moslem holy book) Koran, in the last prayer for the dead."
Benhamouda, a staunch supporter of Zeroual, was gunned down in central Algiers on Tuesday by four men, who the government said were Moslem fundamentalists.

Earlier on Thursday hundreds of mourners paid last respects to Benhamouda, whose body lay in a coffin in the union building Witnesses said early discreet security was beefed up as crowds increased, with elite troops deployed on the roof.
The security was a reminder of other attacks in Algiers and elsewhere which, like Benhamouda's killing, have been blamed by the authorities on Moslem rebels.
Algerian residents and state-run radio said traffic stopped across Algeria at 1 p.m. (1200 GMT) in response to a call by the union to observe one minute of silence for his memory.

At the union building where Benhamouda was gunned down, Algerian television showed his coffin draped in the national green and white flag and surrounded by wreaths, his portrait at one end. Six men from the civil protection service stood guard.
"One elderly woman collapsed in tears as she passed the coffin, while another shouted out 'We will not give way to terrorism'," said Algeria's official news agency APS.
Despite the government blaming Moslem rebels, independent newspapers and many ordinary Algerians asked whether they, or political rivals, were behind the killing.
Benhamouda's last words -- "Kamel, my brother, they have betrayed us" -- gasped out before he died and reported by an Algerian newspaper, added to the mystery.
His final words, the ambush in central Algiers and the escape in the heavily-policed city of the gunmen raised a clamour of questions over his killing and its motives.
Algeria's independent newspapers all asked: "Who killed Benhamouda?", a powerful figure only in his 40s who was preparing to start his own political party.
Liberte asked if he died because he was "the new political man who was preparing...to upset the national chessboard...Who killed him, or rather, who ordered his elimination?"
Benhamouda, a vociferous anti-Islamist, recently said Algeria's political hierarchy had done nothing to resolve five years of crisis in which about 60,000 people have been killed.
The violence began in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists. New elections are promised before July this year.
At El-Alia cemetery, reserved for Algeria's martyrs, one woman said simply: "We lost the father of the poor and the defender of workers' rights."
